title: Conditioning and blending polymer clay
subtitle: How to prepare polymer clay for use and blend colours consistently by hand
excerpt: Polymer clay straight from the packet is stiff and prone to cracking when shaped. Conditioning (working the clay by hand until warm and pliable) is the first step for every polymer project. Blending two colours follows the same kneading and folding process and produces consistent, streak-free colour gradients.
sourceNotes: Polymer clay conditioning and blending derived from first principles.

glossaryTerms.definition: A PVC-based modelling clay that remains workable at room temperature and cures hard at 110-130°C in a domestic oven
Kneading and warming polymer clay until it is soft, smooth, and pliable; the necessary first step before any modelling

content.text: All
polymer clay
needs
conditioning

before use. Unconditioned clay has PVC plasticizers unevenly distributed; it tears, cracks at fold lines, and produces a cured piece with weak spots. A few minutes of hand work changes the clay from stiff to smooth and eliminates the cracking risk.
How to condition polymer clay by hand
Break off the amount you need (no more than 50 g at a time for hand conditioning).
Roll the clay into a log between your palms. The heat from your hands begins softening the clay.
Fold the log in half and roll it into a log again. Repeat this fold-and-roll cycle 20-30 times.
Test readiness: fold the conditioned clay in half. If the fold holds cleanly without cracking at the bend, the clay is ready. A crack means more conditioning is needed.
Very stiff clay can be warmed slightly by rolling it between your palms rapidly for 30 seconds before starting the fold cycle.
Blending two colours into a third
Condition both colours separately first, then blend them. Trying to condition and blend at the same time produces streaky, incompletely mixed colours.
Roll equal amounts of each colour into logs of the same length. Press them side by side.
Twist the combined log to start mixing the colours.
Fold the twisted log and roll it into a log again. Repeat fold-and-roll until the colour is even. 30-50 cycles produces a smooth, streak-free blend for most combinations.

To make a gradient (Skinner blend), stack the two colours as a triangle (one colour at the left, the other at the right) and fold and roll only in one direction. This preserves a gradient from colour A on one end to colour B on the other.
What well-conditioned clay feels like

Well-conditioned clay is warm, smooth, and pliable. It stretches without tearing, bends without cracking, and holds impressions cleanly. It should have no air bubbles; bubbles in unconditioned clay create voids in a cured piece. If you see surface dimples, fold and roll further to work the air out.
Common mistakes
Skipping conditioning. Cured pieces made from unconditioned clay may appear fine but are prone to breaking at fold points or joins.

Over-conditioning very soft clays in warm weather. Clay conditioned too thoroughly in a hot room becomes sticky and loses its shape. Keep work sessions short and rest the clay in a cool place if it becomes too soft.
Blending colours at different conditioning stages. One firm colour and one soft colour will remain unevenly blended. Condition both to the same softness before blending.
